paper.one_line_finding: Dyads that received GPT-4o-mini cues produced ideas with higher topic diversity (entropy 2.3, SD 0.3 vs 2.1, SD 0.4; F(1, 67.03) = 6.51, p = 0.013) and conversations covering more topics (9.6 vs 8.0 unique topics; F(1, 50.76) = 6.25, p = 0.016), with no significant difference in the number of ideas and no printed test of across-group homogenization (PDF pp. 7-9, Sec. 5.1, Fig. 5; PDF p. 17, Fig. 6).

studies.label: Randomized dyadic brainstorming experiment: conversational cues crossed with meeting modality
studies.cluster_se_treatment: Both members of each dyad share the assigned discussion condition. The idea-topic, conversation-topic, and idea-count REML analyses use one group score per dyad. Access-to-Cue, Modality, and their interaction are fixed effects; Prior Design Experience and Recycling Knowledge are random effects. This supports se_basis=cluster for the reported topic-diversity tests because the observational unit is the dyad. No separate cluster-robust standard error is printed. The idea-homogenization analysis instead compares individual idea distances with a Wilcoxon test; neither its numerical result nor an adjustment for ideas nested within dyads is reported. The exact allocation procedure is not described. PDF p. 3 (printed p. 298), Sec. 1; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 300), Sec. 4.1.1; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), Sec. 5.1.1; PDF p. 9 (printed p. 304), Secs. 5.1.2-5.1.3; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 306), Sec. 6.3.

counts_source.quote: We recruited 172 participants, randomly assigned to four conditions; Cue-Virtual, Cue-InPerson, NoCue-Virtual, and NoCue-InPerson to participate in a brainstorming discussion with one other participant (in 86 dyads).

arms.name: Cue-Virtual
arms.description: Dyad partners in separate rooms used CueTip video conferencing and shared notes, receiving automatically generated conversational cues approximately once per minute.

arms.name: Cue-InPerson
arms.description: Dyad partners in the same room used CueTip and shared notes, receiving the same automatically generated conversational cues and notifications.

arms.name: NoCue-Virtual
arms.description: Dyad partners in separate rooms used the same video-conferencing interface and shared notes without conversational cues.

arms.name: NoCue-InPerson
arms.description: Dyad partners in the same room used the same interface and shared notes without conversational cues.

studies.task: Dyads generated alternative uses for recyclable trash from a beach cleanup, recorded ideas as bullet points in shared notes, and selected their best idea (PDF p. 7, printed p. 302, Sec. 4.1.3; PDF p. 15, printed p. 310, App. A.2.2).

ai_tool.name: CueTip using OpenAI GPT-4o-mini
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 300), Secs. 3.2.2, 3.3, and 4.1.2; Appendix A.3.2, PDF pp. 15-16 (printed pp. 310-311). Model release year is not printed.

estimates.outcome: Topic diversity of generated ideas (Shannon entropy per dyad)
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Ideas pooled across groups were clustered using BERTopic with HDBSCAN; Shannon entropy was calculated with scipy. The reported comparison is between dyad scores. This measures topical variety within each dyad, not similarity across different dyads. PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), Sec. 4.1.4; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 303), Fig. 5a.

sources.quote: [F(1, 67.03) = 6.51, p = 0.013] between the groups with cues (μ = 2.3, SD = 0.3) and without cues (μ = 2.1, SD = 0.4)
Groups with cues generated ideas with more topic diversity than groups without cues.

estimates.notes: The test is the REML access-to-cue main effect across modalities. Fixed effects are cue access, modality, and their interaction; random effects are prior design experience and recycling knowledge. The paper also reports a confirming Tukey HSD comparison; the main REML test is recorded here. Reported SDs describe dyad-level scores, not individual participant scores. The specified sd_level vocabulary omits team, so sd_level is null rather than mislabeling these SDs. se_basis is cluster because this analysis uses a score per dyad. Methods describe entropy as each idea’s score, but the results and Fig. 5a compare groups; the exact aggregation is unclear. The dependent-variable wording “topic diversity of cues” in this subsection appears to be an error for ideas, since NoCue groups also have scores. Higher entropy is treated as greater flexibility. Arm counts and numerical SEs or CIs are not printed.

estimates.outcome: Topic diversity of the conversation (distinct broad IAB topics per dyad)
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Assembly AI transcribed the ideation conversation and mapped utterances to Interactive Advertising Bureau topics. The outcome is the combined set of unique broadest-level topics across speakers and conversational rounds, summarized for each dyad. It covers the spoken discussion rather than only the listed ideas. PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), Sec. 4.1.4; PDF p. 9 (printed p. 304), Sec. 5.1.2.

sources.quote: [F(1, 50.76) = 6.25, p = 0.016] between groups with cues (μ = 9.6, SD = 2.2) and groups without cues (μ = 8.0, SD = 2.5)
For all words spoken by the same person in each round of conversation within each group, we measured the number of unique Level 1 topics covered.

estimates.notes: Higher values mean that the dyad’s spoken discussion covers more distinct broad topics; this is coded other rather than overall creativity or across-person diversity. The test is the REML access-to-cue main effect across modalities. Fixed effects are cue access, modality, and their interaction; random effects are prior design experience and recycling knowledge. A confirming Tukey HSD comparison is reported, but the main REML test is recorded here. Reported SDs are across dyad-level conversation scores. The specified sd_level vocabulary omits team, so sd_level is null. se_basis is cluster because the analysis uses a score per dyad. The recording exclusions in footnote 12, PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), do not unambiguously establish the analyzed sample; no count is inferred. Arm counts and numerical SEs or CIs are not printed.

estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Research team members reviewed each dyad’s shared notes, removed duplicates, resolved uncertain idea boundaries with another team member, and filled in missing ideas from recordings and transcripts. The outcome counts the resulting idea points. PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), Sec. 4.1.4.

sources.quote: None of the factors showed a significant difference based on the REML model.
Groups with cues did not generate more ideas than groups without cues.

estimates.notes: The paper reports a REML analysis with cue access, modality, and their interaction as fixed effects, and prior design experience and recycling knowledge as random effects. It concludes that cues did not increase the number of ideas, but prints no arm-specific means, SDs, differences, test statistics, p values, SEs, or CIs for this outcome. The overall mean across all groups in Sec. 5 is not an arm mean and is not entered as one. Retained as an eligible contrast with null numerical fields. se_basis is not_reported because no numerical uncertainty is printed.

estimates.outcome: Idea homogenization across groups (cosine distance to an average idea embedding)
estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Cosine distance between each idea embedding and an average idea embedding; embedding model not stated. Sec. 6.3 describes a separate average within each condition, whereas Appendix A.4.1 describes an average across groups with distances to ideas from both Cue and NoCue groups. Fig. 6 pools the modalities under Cue Ideas and No Cue Ideas. The unit is an idea, not a dyad or a pair of participants. PDF p. 11 (printed p. 306), Sec. 6.3; PDF p. 16 (printed p. 311), Appendix A.4.1; PDF p. 17 (printed p. 312), Fig. 6.

sources.quote: we conducted a Wilcoxon test on the Access-to-Cue factor
between each idea and the average embedding of all ideas within each condition
getting the average embedding based on ideas across groups, and calculate pairwise distances between the average embedding and idea embeddings from both Cue and NoCue groups
The more concentrated distribution of cosine distances suggests that ideas are closer semantically to the group average, indicating lower semantic variability.

estimates.notes: Figure-only numerical result: Fig. 6 shows violin distributions without printed arm summary values. No human-idea arm means, SDs, SEs, analyzed counts, Wilcoxon statistic, p value, or confidence interval is printed. Values inferred from plotted positions are not transcribed. The main text calls the measure cosine similarity, but Fig. 6 explicitly plots cosine distance; higher distance is coded more_diverse. Sec. 6.3 describes condition-specific centroids, while App. A.4.1 describes an average across groups with distances to ideas from both Cue and NoCue groups. The centroid cannot be settled from the paper. A pooled centroid would mix within-arm spread with displacement from the pooled average. The Wilcoxon method is named without its numerical result, so test remains null and se_basis is not_reported. Its observations are individual ideas, with no described adjustment for nesting within dyads. The numerical comparison of original versus Wikipedia-pipeline cues concerns model outputs and is excluded as S2-O1.

open_items: Randomized people and dyads per arm, and analyzed people and dyads per outcome and arm, are not printed. The overall recruited/randomized count must not be substituted for an analysis count; no counts are inferred from degrees of freedom or exclusion arithmetic.

Exclusions differ by analysis. Sec. 4.1.1 excludes sessions for echoes and technical issues, and participants missing background covariates. Footnote 12 additionally describes incomplete recordings but does not settle how those exclusions overlap with its audio-session total. PDF p. 5 (printed p. 300) and PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302).

Printed SDs for idea entropy and conversation topics describe dyad scores. Individual participant SDs are unavailable, and the specified sd_level vocabulary lacks a team category; both sd_level fields are left null with an explicit explanation.

The precise aggregation of idea-topic entropy into the dyad score is unclear: methods refer to each idea’s topic-diversity score while the result is a group comparison. PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), Secs. 4.1.4 and 5.1.1; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 303), Fig. 5a.
Idea-count arm descriptives and numerical test results are not printed. PDF p. 9 (printed p. 304), Sec. 5.1.3.

Idea-homogenization arm levels and uncertainty are not printed. Fig. 6 contains only distributions, and the Wilcoxon test has no reported statistic or p value. PDF p. 11 (printed p. 306), Sec. 6.3; PDF p. 17 (printed p. 312), Fig. 6.

Idea-homogenization embedding model and centroid construction are unresolved: a within-condition average in Sec. 6.3 versus an average across Cue and NoCue groups in Appendix A.4.1. No treatment of dependence among ideas from the same dyad is described.
Random assignment is stated, but the exact allocation procedure and the relation to demographic balancing are not described. PDF p. 5 (printed p. 300), Secs. 4.1.1 and 4.1.3.

Appendix A.3.1 supplies a familiarity-building cue prompt, but whether Cue dyads also received cues during that preliminary task is not stated. PDF p. 15 (printed p. 310); PDF p. 5 (printed p. 300), Sec. 4.1.3.
The model release year and participant country are not stated in the paper; author affiliations alone do not establish participant location.
